name: Risk Management
description: Identifies, measures, monitors, and controls the full spectrum of financial and non-financial risks arising from the bank's lending, trading, and operational activities. Provides the quantitative and qualitative framework that ensures capital adequacy, protects against fraud and operational failure, and satisfies the PRA's requirements for model governance and operational resilience. Risk Management is a mandatory capability for any PRA-authorised firm — it cannot be outsourced in its entirety, though point solutions for data and tooling may be procured externally.
mandate_source: Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) / CRD IV — Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 capital calculations
CRR2 / Basel 3.1 UK transposition — Fundamental Review of Trading Book (FRTB), output floors, revised standardised approaches
PRA Rulebook: Credit Risk, Market Risk, Operational Risk, Internal Ratings Based Approach (IRB)
PRA Supervisory Statement SS3/18 — Model risk management principles (superseded by SS1/23)
PRA Supervisory Statement SS1/23 — Model Risk Management Principles for Banks
PRA Supervisory Statement SS1/21 — Operational Resilience: Impact tolerances for important business services
Bank of England / FCA DP5/22 — Artificial intelligence and machine learning models in financial services
FCA Principles for Business — Principle 2 (Skill, Care and Diligence), Principle 3 (Management and Control)
UK Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) — accountable individuals for risk
Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) — Part IV permissions and threshold conditions

table_stakes: Pillar 1 capital calculation (credit, market, operational risk)
Internal credit ratings and PD/LGD/EAD modelling for corporate and SME lending
Market risk VaR and sensitivities reporting
Basel II/III-era stress testing (ICAAP, PRA concurrent stress tests)
Operational loss data collection and scenario analysis for Op Risk capital
Regulatory reporting: COREP, FINREP capital templates
Basic fraud detection via rule-based transaction monitoring
differentiators: Real-time credit risk re-pricing using ML-based PD models — Zest AI and Scienaptic demonstrate consumer credit accuracy gains of 10-20% over traditional scorecards
FRTB Internal Models Approach (IMA) approval — very few banks globally have achieved this; most expected to fall back to Standardised Approach under UK Basel 3.1
Enterprise-wide risk aggregation across credit, market, and operational risk in a single analytical platform (SAS Risk, Moody's Analytics RiskFoundation)
Behavioural analytics for fraud: Featurespace ARIC platform models individual customer behaviour patterns to detect novel fraud attacks without rule updates
Forward-looking climate risk integration into credit models — NGFS scenario analysis, PRA Climate Capital Guidance
Model risk management as a governed programme rather than an ad-hoc validation activity — SS1/23 compliance at scale
disruptors: Zest AI — ML-based credit underwriting that claims to reduce default rates 25%+ by using non-traditional data features; challenges FICO and traditional scorecard vendors
Scienaptic AI — AI-powered credit decisioning platform used by community banks and credit unions; expanding into commercial credit
Featurespace — unsupervised and adaptive ML for fraud and financial crime detection; deployed at HSBC, NatWest, Worldpay
NetGuardians — AI fraud prevention for commercial and retail banking, focused on payment fraud and internal fraud
Quantexa — contextual intelligence platform for fraud, financial crime, and customer intelligence; network analytics across transactions
DataRobot / H2O.ai — AutoML platforms reducing time-to-production for risk models; threat to SAS and bespoke model development
Resistant AI — document fraud detection and adversarial ML robustness; growing in credit onboarding
Credolab — alternative credit scoring using device metadata and behavioural signals for thin-file borrowers
unbundling: Fraud detection is being unbundled as a specialist capability — Featurespace, NetGuardians, ComplyAdvantage, and Quantexa offer standalone fraud and financial crime platforms that integrate via API rather than requiring a monolithic risk platform
Credit scoring data is commoditising — Experian, Equifax, TransUnion offer bureau scores and attributes as API services; FICO licenses the scorecard methodology separately from data

Model risk management is emerging as a distinct function with its own tooling — ModelOp, ValidMind, and Arthur AI offer model governance, monitoring, and documentation platforms independent of the modelling tool

Stress testing is unbundling from core risk engines — Moody's Analytics AXIS, S&P Global Market Intelligence, and Kamakura offer cloud-based stress testing SaaS that banks connect to rather than running internally
Operational risk frameworks (RCSA, scenario analysis, loss capture) offered standalone by MetricStream, Archer (OpenPages), LogicGate
rebundling: SAS Risk Intelligence suite re-bundles credit risk, market risk, ALM, liquidity, and regulatory capital into a single analytical layer — dominant in Tier 1 and Tier 2 UK banks
Moody's Analytics RiskFoundation re-bundles IRB modelling, stress testing, economic capital, and regulatory reporting
MSCI's acquisition of RCA Analytics and Real Estate data bundles investment risk analytics with real estate credit risk data for commercial banks with CRE portfolios
Temenos and Finastra are embedding risk components into their core banking platforms — trend toward risk-as-a-module within the banking stack rather than standalone risk engines
switching_drivers: Basel 3.1 / FRTB implementation deadlines forcing legacy risk engine replacement — SA-CCR and FRTB Standardised require calculation engines many legacy systems cannot support
PRA SS1/23 model risk management requirements increasing governance overhead on home-grown models — driving demand for validated vendor models or governed ML platforms
Total cost of ownership of legacy SAS implementations — licence cost, specialist consultant dependency, slow upgrade cycles
Real-time fraud pressure — card-not-present and APP fraud losses forcing upgrade from batch to real-time detection

current: CRR/CRD IV — Pillar 1 capital: Standardised and IRB for credit risk, Standardised for market risk, BIA/SA/AMA for operational risk
PRA SS3/18 (now superseded) and SS1/23 — Model Risk Management Principles: model inventory, tiering, validation independence, senior accountability, model risk appetite

PRA SS1/21 — Operational Resilience: important business services identified, impact tolerances set, self-assessment complete by March 2022, severe but plausible scenario testing ongoing. PRA supervision now focused on testing quality, evidence of remediation, and board-level ownership
EBA Guidelines on ICT and Security Risk — now onshored under PRA/FCA expectations
Bank of England DP5/22 — AI/ML model governance: expectations of explainability, bias testing, data lineage, human oversight, stress testing of ML models under distribution shift
PRA ICAAP and Pillar 2 framework — Pillar 2A add-ons for IRB model risk, pension risk, concentration risk, interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB)
incoming_2_3_years: Basel 3.1 UK implementation — PRA CP16/22 finalised as PS17/23: FRTB Standardised Approach mandatory by 1 January 2026 (UK implementation date), Internal Models Approach (IMA) requires PRA approval. Output floors phase-in begins at 50% (2025) rising to 72.5% (2030). Significant capital impact for IRB banks — floor-constrained banks see 10-30% RWA increase

FRTB full implementation — Sensitivity-Based Approach (SBA) for market risk replacing VaR/sVaR; requires new sensitivities infrastructure, new P&L attribution testing, new desk-level approval process. Legacy VaR systems cannot support SBA without significant re-engineering

Credit Risk SA revision under Basel 3.1 — risk-weight changes for real estate, equity, specialised lending. UK implementation PS17/23 aligns broadly with Basel, with some PRA-specific adjustments for UK CRE market

PRA AI/ML model governance expectations — DP5/22 is a discussion paper; supervisory expectations paper expected 2025-2026. Likely to require: model cards for all material ML models, bias and fairness testing documentation, explainability standards, ongoing performance monitoring, model risk appetite for AI-specific risks (hallucination, distribution shift, adversarial inputs)

Operational Resilience post-March 2025 supervisory focus — SS1/21 deadline passed; PRA/FCA now in supervisory assessment phase. Banks that cannot evidence scenario testing results and remediation programmes should expect 166 letters. Focus shifting to third-party concentration risk and cloud resilience

DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) — applies to UK branches of EU firms and UK firms operating in EU. ICT third-party risk management, register of critical ICT providers, ICT-related incident reporting. UK equivalent via FSMA amendments and FCA/PRA operational resilience framework convergence
enforcement_signals: PRA Dear CEO letters on model risk (2022-2023) — increasing expectations on model inventory completeness, validation independence, and SS1/23 implementation plans. Several Tier 2 banks received private feedback on gaps

PRA FRTB readiness reviews — PRA conducted desk-by-desk reviews of trading book classification in 2023; banks with poorly evidenced BNDF boundary decisions face desk-level approval risk under FRTB IMA

FCA/PRA operational resilience supervisory assessments 2023-2024 — public speeches from David Bailey (PRA) signalling that operational resilience testing evidence quality is below expectations for a subset of firms; cloud concentration is a specific concern

BoE/FCA AI governance discussion paper DP5/22 follow-up — July 2024 joint feedback statement noted industry concern about explainability requirements; regulators signalling proportionate approach to model complexity vs explainability trade-off, but expecting clear risk appetite statements

platform_options: SAS Risk Intelligence — credit risk, market risk, ALM, regulatory capital, stress testing. Dominant in UK Tier 1/2. Heavy licence cost; deep PRA familiarity. Migration risk high.
Moody's Analytics RiskFoundation (formerly ERISK) — IRB modelling, ECL/IFRS 9, stress testing, regulatory capital. Strong in mid-market UK banks.
MSCI RiskManager — market risk analytics, VaR, sensitivities, FRTB SA calculations. Strong for banks with significant trading books.
Murex MX.3 — front-to-back trading system with embedded market risk and FRTB SA/IMA modules. Buy if already on Murex for front office.
Finastra Kondor — legacy treasury/risk platform; declining install base but still in several mid-market UK banks.
Experian PowerCurve / FICO Platform — credit decisioning and scorecard management for retail and SME lending. Buy for decisioning; build the underlying credit risk framework.
Zest AI / Scienaptic — ML credit underwriting. Buy as a wrapper over bureau data for thin-file or small business lending; requires bank to own model validation.
Featurespace ARIC — real-time fraud and financial crime detection. Strong buy candidate — specialist capability, PRA-familiar, proven in UK market.
NetGuardians — fraud prevention, internal fraud focus. Niche buy for commercial banks with internal fraud risk.
Quantexa — network analytics for fraud and financial crime. Buy for complex commercial fraud or AML network analysis.
ModelOp / ValidMind / Arthur AI — model governance and monitoring platforms. Buy to operationalise SS1/23 compliance rather than building governance tooling in-house.

Archer (OpenPages, now IBM) / MetricStream / LogicGate — operational risk management platforms (RCSA, loss capture, scenario analysis). Buy for OpRisk framework; integrate with capital calculation engine.
Moody's CreditView / S&P Global Market Intelligence — external credit data and probability of default benchmarks. Buy as data inputs to internal credit models.
Kamakura KRIS / SAS Stress Testing — scenario-based stress testing engines. Buy or use as validation benchmark alongside internal stress test models.
must_build_in_house: Credit risk appetite and policy — the bank's own lending criteria, sector limits, and concentration limits must be authored internally; no vendor can define risk appetite

IRB model development for PRA approval — PRA requires the bank to own, understand, and be accountable for IRB models; vendor-supplied models must be fully validated and owned by the bank's model risk function
ICAAP narrative and Pillar 2 assessment — PRA requires board-owned capital adequacy assessment; cannot be outsourced
Model risk governance programme — model inventory, tiering, validation independence, risk appetite per SS1/23 — governance framework must be internal
Operational resilience programme — identification of important business services, impact tolerances, scenario design — PRA requires board accountability and internal ownership
Fraud strategy and rules governance — specific fraud typology rules and thresholds must be owned by the bank; vendor platforms provide the detection engine, not the strategy
buy_candidates: Fraud detection engine — Featurespace, NetGuardians, or Quantexa as a real-time detection platform via API integration; avoids competing with specialist AI investment
Credit bureau data and scores — Experian, Equifax, TransUnion as data inputs; commoditised and cost-effective
FRTB Standardised Approach calculation engine — MSCI, Murex, or vendor SA engine rather than building SBA sensitivities infrastructure from scratch
Operational risk management platform — Archer or MetricStream for RCSA, loss database, scenario analysis; saves GRC platform build
Model governance tooling — ValidMind or ModelOp to operationalise SS1/23 requirements; avoids bespoke governance tool build
Stress testing scenario service — Moody's or S&P scenario libraries for ICAAP and IFRS 9 staging; use as benchmark inputs rather than building macro scenario models

primary_revenue_streams: Risk Management is a cost centre and regulatory prerequisite — it does not generate direct revenue
Effective credit risk management enables higher-quality loan book growth, directly sustaining net interest income (NII)
Strong fraud detection reduces operational losses and directly protects fee income from commercial payment services
Capital efficiency from optimised IRB models reduces RWA for performing assets, freeing capital for higher-return deployment
Operational resilience track record supports client confidence in commercial banking services, sustaining deposit franchise and fee income
margin_pressure: Basel 3.1 output floors — floor-constrained IRB banks will see RWA inflation of 10-30% on qualifying portfolios, compressing RoE on affected segments
FRTB implementation cost — industry estimates GBP 50-200m for major UK banks; significant ongoing infrastructure cost for trading book market risk
Fraud losses rising — APP fraud and CNP fraud losses continue to grow; Payment Systems Regulator mandatory reimbursement rules (effective October 2024) shift more loss to banks
SS1/23 model risk compliance — additional model validation headcount and governance overhead increasing model development cycle times and cost
Legacy risk system technical debt — SAS and Murex upgrade costs, specialist consultant dependency, slow release cycles
cross_sell_hooks: Strong credit risk capability enables expansion into specialised lending products (leveraged finance, project finance, CRE) which carry higher margins
Fraud detection investment supports onboarding of higher-risk SME and fintech clients who would otherwise be declined
Operational resilience maturity enables the bank to offer operational resilience assurance to corporate treasury clients as a differentiator
Model risk governance capability creates optionality to offer model validation services to smaller banks or building societies as a fee-based service

sub_capabilities.name: Credit Risk
sub_capabilities.description: Assesses, prices, and monitors the risk that borrowers — corporate, SME, and financial institution counterparties — will default on their obligations. Encompasses origination credit analysis, internal credit ratings (including IRB PD/LGD/EAD models), credit approval governance, portfolio monitoring, IFRS 9 expected credit loss provisioning, and sector/concentration limit management.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Credit Risk is the definitional core of a lending bank's risk function — no major player treats it as separate from the broader Risk Management capability. Vendor platforms (SAS, Moody's) bundle it alongside market and operational risk. The IRB approval process under CRR/CRD IV and the ICAAP under Pillar 2 are joint credit-market-operational risk assessments. Credit scoring data vendors (Experian, FICO) are data inputs, not replacements for the credit risk capability itself. Participants (credit analysts, credit committee, PRA) are the same as the parent. The lifecycle (origination → monitoring → provisioning → workout) is a sub-set of the lending lifecycle, not an independent one. Scalability is driven by loan volume, identical to parent. Decision: RETAIN within Risk Management.

sub_capabilities.name: Market Risk
sub_capabilities.description: Measures and limits the bank's exposure to adverse movements in interest rates, FX rates, credit spreads, and equity prices arising from trading book and banking book positions. Includes VaR/FRTB sensitivity-based approach calculations, PnL attribution, IRRBB modelling for banking book interest rate risk, stress testing of market positions, and limit monitoring against the bank's market risk appetite.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Market Risk is integral to the bank's treasury and trading operations and is co-governed with Credit Risk under the same CRR/CRD capital framework (COREP). FRTB changes the calculation methodology but not the organisational home — it remains within Risk Management. Vendor platforms (MSCI, Murex, Finastra) offer market risk modules as part of broader risk suites rather than standalone products. The participants are internal (Treasury, Trading desk, Risk function) and the PRA — no distinct external participant set beyond what the parent capability already has. IRRBB for banking book and VaR for trading book have different metrics but the same governance and reporting cadence. Decision: RETAIN within Risk Management.

sub_capabilities.name: Operational Risk
sub_capabilities.description: Identifies, assesses, and controls risks arising from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems, or from external events. Covers the RCSA (Risk and Control Self-Assessment) programme, operational loss event capture, scenario analysis for tail OpRisk events, operational risk capital calculation (Basel Standardised Approach post-Basel 3.1), and the governance of the operational risk appetite statement.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Operational Risk sits squarely within the three lines of defence model and is integrated with the bank's credit and market risk capital framework under Pillar 1 and Pillar 2. While GRC platform vendors (Archer, MetricStream) offer standalone OpRisk products, these are tooling decisions, not capability separation signals. The Basel Standardised Approach (replacing AMA post-Basel 3.1) makes OpRisk capital calculation less model-intensive and more data-driven — no separation signal. The participants (1LoD business owners, 2LoD risk function, internal audit, PRA) are the same as the parent risk capability. Decision: RETAIN within Risk Management.

sub_capabilities.name: Fraud Detection
sub_capabilities.description: Detects, prevents, and investigates fraudulent activity across all channels and product lines — including payment fraud (authorised push payment, card fraud, CHAPS, SWIFT), identity fraud at onboarding, internal fraud, and cyber-enabled fraud. Operates in real-time against transaction flows and uses behavioural analytics, network graph analysis, and rule-based scoring to generate fraud alerts for investigation.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Fraud Detection meets all four promotion criteria and has a strong market signal for promotion to standalone capability. (1) Distinct participants: Fraud operations involves specialist fraud investigation teams, liaison with Action Fraud, Cifas, National Fraud Intelligence Bureau, PSR (Payment Systems Regulator), and fraud analytics vendors — participants not present in credit or market risk. The PSR's mandatory APP fraud reimbursement regime (effective October 2024) creates a direct regulator relationship specific to fraud. (2) Separate regulatory framework: The PSR APP fraud reimbursement rules (PS23/3), the FCA's Transaction Monitoring requirements under the Money Laundering Regulations, and Cifas membership obligations constitute a separate regulatory and industry body framework distinct from the CRR capital framework governing credit and market risk. PSD2/PSR liability rules for unauthorised payments add further distinct regulation. (3) Distinct lifecycle: Fraud detection runs in real-time (milliseconds) at transaction execution — a fundamentally different operational tempo from credit risk (days to weeks) or OpRisk (annual RCSA cycles). The lifecycle is detect → alert → investigate → recover → report, with real-time SLA requirements that have no parallel in the credit or market risk lifecycle. (4) Independent scalability: Fraud transaction volumes are driven by payment volumes and attack campaign intensity — completely independent of loan book size or market position. Real-time ML fraud models must scale to peak payment throughput (potentially millions of transactions per day) with sub-100ms latency. The specialist vendors (Featurespace ARIC, NetGuardians, Quantexa) are evidence of an independent industry segment. Decision: PROMOTE to standalone capability.

sub_capabilities.name: Model Risk
sub_capabilities.description: Governs the bank's portfolio of quantitative models — encompassing model inventory management, tiering and materiality assessment, independent model validation, model performance monitoring, and the model risk appetite statement. Provides the governance framework required by PRA SS1/23 and ensures model risk is treated as a distinct risk type with board-level accountability under SM&CR.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Model Risk is an emerging distinct discipline — PRA SS1/23 gives it explicit governance requirements and there are now dedicated tooling vendors (ModelOp, ValidMind, Arthur AI). However, market structure does not yet support promotion. Model Risk Management is a governance layer over all quantitative models used across risk, finance, and treasury — it does not own the underlying models or operate independently of the capabilities whose models it governs. Its participants are internal (model developers, validators, CRO, board risk committee) plus the PRA model risk team — the same stakeholder set as the parent risk function. The lifecycle (develop → validate → approve → monitor → decommission) is a governance cycle over the models within credit, market, and operational risk, not a standalone institutional process. ValidMind and ModelOp are governance tooling choices, not evidence of capability separation. Retained here but expected to grow in scope and governance maturity as SS1/23 expectations develop. Decision: RETAIN within Risk Management.

design_decisions.decision: Promote Fraud Detection to standalone capability (CAP-004.04 → separate CAP)
design_decisions.rationale: Fraud Detection meets all four promotion criteria with strong market evidence. The PSR APP fraud mandatory reimbursement regime (October 2024) creates a board-level liability and a direct PSR regulatory relationship that has no equivalent in credit or market risk. Real-time ML detection at transaction scale requires infrastructure (sub-100ms latency, high-throughput event processing) that is architecturally incompatible with overnight batch credit risk engines. Specialist vendors (Featurespace, NetGuardians, Quantexa) confirm the market has unbundled this capability. Retaining fraud detection inside Risk Management would force a deployment unit that must serve both annual ICAAP cycles and real-time payment processing — a fundamental tension in NFRs.
alternatives_considered: Retain Fraud Detection inside Risk Management as a sub-capability
Merge Fraud Detection with Compliance & Regulatory / Financial Crime
design_decisions.rejected_because: Retaining inside Risk Management ignores the real-time vs batch NFR conflict and the distinct regulatory framework (PSR vs PRA CRR). Merging with Compliance/Financial Crime conflates fraud prevention (operational, real-time) with AML monitoring (regulatory, investigative) — different participants, different SLAs, different regulatory frameworks. Fraud Detection must be standalone.

design_decisions.decision: Retain Model Risk within Risk Management despite emerging governance tooling market
design_decisions.rationale: PRA SS1/23 gives Model Risk explicit regulatory backing and there is a growing vendor ecosystem (ModelOp, ValidMind). However, Model Risk is a governance discipline over the bank's quantitative models rather than an operational capability with its own data domain and business process. It does not have distinct external participants, its lifecycle is tied to the model development cycles within credit and market risk, and its scalability is driven by the number of models rather than an independent demand driver. As SS1/23 implementation matures and the AI/ML governance regime evolves (DP5/22 successor paper expected 2025-2026), this decision should be re-evaluated.
alternatives_considered: Promote Model Risk to standalone capability given SS1/23 senior accountability requirements
Absorb Model Risk into Compliance & Regulatory as a governance function
design_decisions.rejected_because: Promoting Model Risk creates a capability that owns no data and has no business process independent of the models it governs — it would be a pure governance overlay, not a deployment boundary. Absorbing into Compliance risks losing the quantitative expertise concentration and the direct PRA CRO accountability line required under SS1/23.

design_decisions.decision: Scope Risk Management to financial risk and governance; exclude IT/cyber risk which sits in Technology Operations
design_decisions.rationale: Operational Risk within Risk Management covers business process, people, and external event risks per the Basel Op Risk framework. IT and cyber risk, while categorised as operational risk for capital purposes, is operationally owned by the CISO function and Technology Operations capability. The PRA's operational resilience framework (SS1/21) and the FCA's SYSC 13-15 requirements on operational risk create a governance connection, but the technical ownership and day-to-day management of IT risk belongs in Technology Operations. Risk Management receives IT risk metrics and scenarios as inputs to the ICAAP but does not own cyber controls.
alternatives_considered: Include cyber and IT risk within Risk Management (Operational Risk sub-capability)
Create a separate Operational Resilience capability
design_decisions.rejected_because: Including cyber/IT risk in Risk Management creates a capability that spans two very different specialist domains — financial risk quantification and technical security controls. The build-vs-buy, talent, and tooling requirements are incompatible. A separate Operational Resilience capability is plausible given SS1/21 maturity, but for a commercial bank of this scale it is premature — the important business services framework and scenario testing can be governed from within Risk Management and Technology Operations jointly. Reviewed as a promotion candidate at Gate 1.

design_decisions.decision: FRTB Standardised Approach targeted as build-vs-buy decision point — vendor SA engine preferred over internal build
design_decisions.rationale: The UK Basel 3.1 implementation mandates FRTB SA for all banks (IMA requires separate PRA approval). Building a Sensitivity-Based Approach calculation engine from scratch requires specialist quant and technology investment that competes with specialist vendors (MSCI, Murex FRTB module, Bloomberg MARS) who have already built and validated these engines for PRA use. For a commercial bank without an active IMA application, buying or licensing a FRTB SA engine is the cost-dominant strategy. The bank must own the input data quality, position feeds, and governance; not the calculation kernel.
alternatives_considered: Build FRTB SA calculation engine in-house using open-source quant libraries
Apply for IMA and invest in internal models infrastructure
design_decisions.rejected_because: Building in-house competes with specialist vendor investment in a non-differentiating calculation layer. IMA application requires multi-year PRA engagement, desk-level approval, and ongoing validation — appropriate only for banks with significant trading book revenues where IMA capital savings justify the investment. A UK commercial bank without material trading operations should not pursue IMA.
